<p class="paper-lede">A message built on authority made people more likely to choose the sustainable product,
and it worked just as well in Ecuador as in Norway. In a field experiment with 346 people, the authority
message outperformed both a commitment-and-consistency message and no message at all.</p>

</section>

<section class="paper-section">
  <h2>The question</h2>
  <p>Most research on nudging people towards sustainable choices comes from Western countries, with very little
    from Latin America. That leaves an open question for anyone designing a sustainability message: does a
    persuasion principle that works in one culture work in another with different values? We tested two
    well-established principles of social influence, authority and commitment-and-consistency, side by side in
    Ecuador and Norway.</p>
</section>

<section class="paper-section">
  <h2>What we found</h2>
  <ol class="findings">
    <li><strong>Persuasion messages increased sustainable choices.</strong> Taken together, the two message
      conditions raised the likelihood of choosing the fairtrade option compared with the control group, as
      preregistered.</li>
    <li><strong>Country made no difference.</strong> Against our second preregistered prediction, the effect of the
      messages did not differ between Ecuador and Norway.</li>
    <li><strong>Authority did most of the work.</strong> The authority message was considerably more effective
      than both the commitment-and-consistency message and the control, in both countries, regardless of how much
      participants trusted authorities or how strongly they needed to be consistent.</li>
  </ol>
</section>

<section class="paper-section">
  <h2>Implications</h2>
  <div class="implications">
    <div>
      <h3>Practical implications</h3>
      <p>Retailers, brands and public agencies that want shoppers to pick the more sustainable product can use
        an authority-based message at the point of choice. The same type of message raised fairtrade choices in
        both Ecuador and Norway, so a single principle can underpin campaigns in markets with very different
        cultural profiles.</p>
    </div>
    <div>
      <h3>Theoretical implications</h3>
      <p>Social influence principles are not interchangeable: authority outperformed commitment-and-consistency,
        and neither trust in authorities nor need for consistency explained the difference. The absence of
        country moderation questions the assumption that persuasion effects are culturally contingent, using
        rare field evidence from Latin America.</p>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>
